title: Psychic Practice, Step by Step
subtitle: A Workbook for Beginners, from First Hunch to Trusted Insight
thesis: Intuition becomes a practice, not a string of lucky moments, when it is worked in short, safe sessions that open and close the same way and end with something written down and honestly checked. A workbook that asks for something different on every page, from a profile of the senses to score sheets, logs and a dictionary of the reader's own symbols, turns scattered hunches into a record the reader can read back and learn to weigh.
back_cover:
You have already had the hunch, the dream that came true, the call you knew was coming. This workbook shows you what to do next, pen in hand.

Psychic Practice, Step by Step is for beginners who have read an introduction or two and still don't know what to do, in what order, or how to tell whether it's working. Every session opens and closes with the same short routine to ground, center and set your boundaries. The rest happens on the page: a profile of your strongest intuitive sense and exercises for each sense, ways to tell a true hunch from fear or wishful thinking, simple experiments you run alone and score honestly, a symbol dictionary built from your own impressions, logs for dreams and signs, partner exercises with clear ethics, and a guided meditation to meet a guide with discernment.

No tarot, no pendulums, no blank journal pages: every page asks for something different, and the only instrument is your own perception. This book doesn't promise powers, accuracy or results. It gives you a method, a safe frame and an honest record of your progress, and at the end you design a routine that is yours to keep.

chapters.title: The Experiences You Have Already Had
chapters.summary: The reader takes stock of the hunches, dreams that came true and moments of knowing they have already lived, and learns a simple framework to name each kind. It comes first because the practice starts from the reader's own history, and it closes by setting personal intentions and honest expectations before any exercise begins.
beats: A few warm paragraphs on why these experiences are worth writing down: they are the reader's starting material, not a test of whether they are gifted.

Experience Inventory: a tick-and-describe sheet of common experiences (a hunch that turned out right, a dream that came true, knowing who is calling before looking, thinking of someone just before they get in touch, sensing the mood of a room), each with space for when it happened, what happened and how it felt.

The Naming Key: a simple framework of five names (hunch, knowing, dream that came true, connection at a distance, sensing an atmosphere) and a sorting grid where the reader files every inventory entry under its name.

Intentions page: sentence starters for why the reader is practicing, which days and how many minutes they will give it, and what they will count as progress (showing up, noticing, writing it down) before any result exists.
Honest expectations: a short checklist of what this practice offers and what it does not (no powers, no accuracy rates, no deadlines), which the reader signs as an agreement with themselves.
Going further: experienced practitioners add a column for how they responded to each experience at the time and mark the ones they have never told anyone about.

chapters.title: Ground, Center and Set Your Boundaries
chapters.summary: This chapter teaches the opening half of the session frame used before every exercise in the book: grounding, centering and setting energetic boundaries. It sits this early because no exercise starts until the reader can settle, feel steady and decide what they let in.
beats: Why every session opens and closes the same way, and the practical setup: a quiet place at home, a set time, a short session, phone away, pen ready.

Guided opening in numbered steps: feet on the floor, slow breath, a grounding image of roots or a cord into the earth, gathering attention to the center of the body, then an energetic boundary set with a clear spoken intention.

Boundary Image Menu: a page of images to choose from (a ring of light, a garden wall, a cloak, a closed door), a box to sketch or describe the reader's own, and a line for the words they will use to set it.

Settling Scale: three practice runs of the opening, each rating restlessness and steadiness before and after on a simple scale, with a different question for each run (what helped, what distracted, what the body did).
Going further: hold the grounded state for longer, try the opening standing or with eyes open, and practice it somewhere ordinary such as a bus or a queue.

chapters.title: Close Down and Learn the Frame by Heart
chapters.summary: The second half of the session frame: gathering energy back, closing down, clearing and returning to ordinary attention, then joining both halves into a checklist the reader can follow from memory. Without a closing, practice spills into the rest of the day; with it, every later chapter has a safe container.
beats: Guided closing in numbered steps: drawing attention back in, closing down the openness of the session, clearing with a physical action (shaking out the hands, washing them, a glass of water) and returning by naming what is in the room.
Session Frame card: the whole opening and closing sequence on one checklist page, meant to sit beside the reader during every exercise in the book.
Recall drill: a blank frame with only the step numbers, filled in from memory and corrected against the card, then repeated on another day with the steps listed out of order to put back in sequence.
Short-version builder: a page for designing a quick open-and-close for busy days, deciding which steps can be shortened and which are never skipped.
Going further: a closing after everyday moments that leave the reader feeling crowded or drained, such as a busy shop, a party or a hard conversation.

chapters.title: Hunch, Fear, Hope, Memory or Imagination?
chapters.summary: This chapter shows how an intuitive impression differs from fear, wishful thinking, memory and imagination, the four voices most often mistaken for it. It comes before any testing because a reader who cannot tell these apart will count noise as insight.
beats: Short portraits of the five voices, with the reassurance that anxiety and wishful thinking are normal and that noticing them is part of the skill, not a failure.

Five Voices table: rows for how each voice arrives (speed, tone, emotional charge, insistence, what it seems to want), partly filled with the book's descriptions and completed with the reader's own examples.

Which Voice? exercise: a dozen short everyday scenarios (dread before a trip, a name that pops into mind, a warm certainty about a new acquaintance, a scene replayed from childhood) that the reader labels, followed by notes on the clues in each.
Hunch post-mortem: a guided page that takes a past hunch that turned out wrong and one that turned out right, and asks which voice each really was and what gave it away.
Going further: practitioners who already give readings review a recent session and mark where a voice other than intuition may have spoken.

chapters.title: Map Where Intuition Lives in Your Body
chapters.summary: The reader maps where intuition, fear and desire show up physically, then carries that map into ordinary days with a comparison log. It follows the five voices because body signals are the quickest way to tell them apart in the moment.
beats: Why the body often registers an impression before the mind names it, and the signals beginners commonly describe (a pull in the gut, a tight chest, warmth, tingling at the back of the neck).
Body-signal map: a printed figure of front and back body outlines on which the reader marks, with a different symbol for each, where a true hunch, a fear and a wish have been felt.
Signal key: a legend page where the reader defines their symbols and describes each sensation in a few words (temperature, weight, movement, speed).

Comparison log for daily life: a week of entries with a different prompt each day (a decision, a person, a place, a message, a route), recording the impression, where in the body it was felt, which voice it seemed to be and what happened.
End-of-week reading: three questions that set the log against the map and redraw the map where the body said something unexpected.
Going further: repeat the body scan at different times of day for a single signal and note how it shifts.

chapters.title: Find Your Strongest Intuitive Sense
chapters.summary: A self-profile of the intuitive senses (seeing, hearing, feeling and knowing, plus smell and taste) shows the reader which channel is strongest for them and which is quietest. It opens the senses section so the reader knows where to start and what to strengthen in the chapters that follow.
beats: A brief sketch of each sense as beginners meet it: pictures on an inner screen, words or tones, bodily sensations and emotions, sudden certainty, and smells or tastes with no source.

Self-profile questionnaire: statements grouped by sense and drawn from everyday life (recalling faces, replaying conversations, sensing a room before walking in), each scored on a simple never-to-often scale.
Profile chart: the reader totals each sense, shades a bar for it and names a strongest channel, a supporting channel and a quiet channel.
Where to start: a reading route that sends the reader first to the exercises for their strongest sense, then to the quietest, with a word on why every sense is worth some time.
Going further: a second profile drawn from the Experience Inventory, noting which sense carried each past experience, compared with the questionnaire result.

chapters.title: Seeing: Train Your Inner Screen
chapters.summary: Exercises for the seeing sense, from holding a simple image steady in the mind's eye to letting an unplanned image arrive and recording it before the mind explains it away. It comes first among the sense exercises because images are where many people first notice impressions, and the skill returns in the envelope tests.
beats: Inner screen warm-up: a guided exercise that builds a familiar object in the mind's eye, changes its size and color, turns it around, then lets it fade.

Open window exercise: inside the session frame, the reader asks to be shown an image about something small and checkable later that day, such as what will be on the kitchen table tonight, and records whatever appears.
Sketch-first sheet: framed boxes for quick drawings, with space underneath for what the reader assumed it meant, so the raw image and the interpretation stay apart.
Detail recall drill: picture a room just left (shapes, light, objects out of place), list what comes, then go back and compare.
Going further: hold an image with eyes open on a blank wall, or let a still inner scene begin to move and follow it.

chapters.title: Hearing: Catch the Quiet Inner Voice
chapters.summary: Exercises for the hearing sense: layered listening to the room and then to the quieter inner voice, and a way to tell a received word from the reader's own self-talk. It follows seeing so the reader can compare the two channels and notice which answers more readily.
beats: Layered listening: a guided exercise that moves attention from distant sounds to near sounds, to the breath, to silence, and then waits.
Single word exercise: after a simple question, the reader waits for one word, a name, a tone or a snatch of music and writes it down before thinking about it.
Word catch page: short entries for each received word or phrase, with its qualities (whose voice, loud or soft, inside or outside the head, familiar or new).
Self-talk check: a page that sets each received word beside the reader's usual inner commentary, to spot differences in tone, speed and vocabulary.
Going further: songs that arrive unbidden, logged with the line that stuck and what was happening that day.

chapters.title: Feeling, Smell and Taste: The Body Senses
chapters.summary: Exercises for the feeling sense, where impressions arrive as bodily sensation or emotion, and for the rarer channels of smell and taste. It sits here because feeling is the sense many readers already use without naming it, and smell and taste tend to arrive the same way, through the body.
beats: Room reading: the reader steps into each room at home and notes its felt quality (warm, heavy, busy, still), then tries the same in a place they know less well.
Energy between the palms: a guided exercise that brings the hands slowly together and apart and records what is felt in the space between them.

Is this mine? log: when a mood or sensation arrives out of nowhere, the reader notes it, asks whether it belongs to them, to someone nearby or to a place, and uses the closing to let go of what is not theirs.
Smell and taste: a scent-memory exercise (recall a smell vividly, then notice what arrives uninvited) and a note page for sudden smells or tastes with no source and what the reader linked them to.
Going further: read the felt quality of a public place, such as a library or a park, at two different times and compare.

chapters.title: Knowing: Tell Certainty From a Guess
chapters.summary: Exercises for the sense of simply knowing something without knowing how. It closes the senses section because knowing is the easiest sense to confuse with guessing, and the reader now has the tools to tell them apart.
beats: What knowing feels like for many people: quiet, complete, arriving all at once, often without images or words.

First-answer drill: a quick run of small questions the reader can check later the same day (which of three friends will reply first, how many messages will be waiting after lunch, the color of the first car to pass), answered within seconds and written down before reasoning starts.
Knowing or guessing page: for the same question, the reader records both a knowing and a deliberate guess, then marks which turned out closer.
Certainty meter: each knowing is rated for how certain it felt at the time and marked later for what happened, to see whether felt certainty and outcome travel together for this reader.
Going further: note the first thing the reader knows about the day on waking and check it in the evening.

chapters.title: Colors, Calls and Honest Scoring
chapters.summary: This chapter teaches the scoring method used in every experiment that follows (hit, near miss, miss) and applies it to the first two low-stakes tests the reader can run alone: colors and who is calling. It opens the testing section because how a score is read matters more than the score itself.
beats: Scoring key: plain definitions of a hit, a near miss and a miss, worked examples, and the rule of writing the impression down before checking so the target cannot move afterwards.
Color test sheet: a few colored cards shuffled face down; for each, the reader records an impression before turning it, with columns for impression, card and score.
Who is calling log: for incoming calls and messages, the reader writes a name before looking and scores it on the same key.

Reading results honestly: why a handful of hits means little on its own, why near misses carry information, and how to log a miss without self-deception and without discouragement; the scores are personal feedback for the reader, not a verdict on psychic ability.
Going further: add a second impression for each color card, such as a feeling or a temperature, and score it separately to see which sense helps.

chapters.title: Sealed Envelopes and Objects in the Hand
chapters.summary: Two more experiments the reader can run alone: sealed envelopes holding a picture or a word, and an object with an unknown story held in the hand. It follows the scoring chapter because both tests use the same honest key, and it ends with a running record that shows the reader their own pattern over time.
beats: Envelope setup in numbered steps: choosing simple targets, wrapping each in dark paper so nothing shows through, sealing, shuffling and marking the envelopes so the reader cannot know which is which.
Envelope sheet: a box to sketch and describe the impression for each envelope before it is opened, then the target, the score and which sense carried the impression.

Object in the hand: the reader holds an object whose story they do not know but a relative or friend can tell them later (an inherited ornament, a second-hand book), records impressions about its places and uses, not messages from anyone, then checks them with that person's agreement on a sheet laid out by sense.
Running record: a page that gathers the scores from every test so far, by test, by sense and by time of day, so the reader looks for a pattern across sessions instead of judging any single session.
Going further: ask a friend to prepare the envelopes so even the setup is blind to the reader.

chapters.title: Ask a Question an Impression Can Answer
chapters.summary: This chapter shows how to phrase a clear question an impression can answer, and how impressions arrive as images, words or sensations. It comes before the symbol dictionary because a vague question produces impressions no dictionary can translate.
beats: What makes a question workable: open rather than yes-or-no, about the reader's own life, specific in time and place, and never about health, legal matters or money.
Question workshop: vague questions rewritten step by step into clear, answerable ones, followed by a page where the reader rewrites a few of their own.
Arrival log: the same clear question asked across several sessions, recording each time whether the answer came as an image, a word or a sensation and how its form changed.
Raw versus read: a two-step page that keeps the impression exactly as it came apart from its interpretation, so meaning is added only at the end and can be revised.
Going further: a question ladder that narrows a broad question in stages and records which stage drew the clearest impression.

chapters.title: Build a Symbol Dictionary of Your Own
chapters.summary: The reader starts a personal symbol dictionary built from their own impressions rather than a borrowed list, recording what each recurring image, word or sensation has pointed to in their practice. It sits at the end of the testing section because the dictionary draws on the sketches, sheets and logs the reader has already filled in.
beats: Why borrowed symbol lists mislead: the same image (a key, a bird, an open door) can mean different things to different people, so a meaning is earned through the reader's own record.
Symbol entry cards: for each symbol, what it looked or felt like, when it first appeared, what it turned out to point to, and how settled the meaning feels so far.

Dictionary pages grouped by kind (images, words and sounds, body sensations, smells and tastes), each group with its own prompts, so the dictionary keeps growing as the reader works through the rest of the book.
Symbol review: a page to revisit each entry after more sessions and mark whether its meaning held, shifted or faded.
Going further: trace a single symbol back through every sheet filled in so far and write its history in a few lines.

chapters.title: Remember Your Dreams and Log Them
chapters.summary: Recall techniques and a dream log whose prompts change from page to page help the reader catch dreams before they fade and notice which ones seem to connect with waking life. It opens the wider practice because dreams keep arriving whether or not the reader sits down to practice.
beats: Recall techniques in numbered steps: an intention before sleep, a pen and notebook by the bed, staying still on waking, writing fragments first and the story second.
Dream log with changing prompts: each entry asks something different (the strongest image, a person, a place, the feeling on waking, a phrase heard, anything that seemed to be about the day ahead).
Dream-to-day check: a short evening column for anything in the day that echoed the dream, noted without forcing a link.
The dreams that feel different: clarity, emotional tone and a sense of being shown something, marked on each entry so they can be found later.
Unsettling dreams: dreams about illness, death or danger are recorded but not treated as predictions, with a calm reset and the closing routine for the morning after.
Going further: set a specific question before sleep and log what the night brings back.

chapters.title: Track Signs and Review Them Weeks Later
chapters.summary: A sign log for synchronicities (repeated numbers, names, songs, chance meetings) and a structured way to review both the sign log and the dream log weeks later to see what held up. It follows the dream log because a review only works once there is a record to look back on.
beats: What counts as a sign in this practice: a meaningful coincidence noticed and written down at the time, not searched for afterwards.
Sign log with changing prompts: entries that ask in turn what was noticed, what the reader was thinking about just before, how it felt and whether it came back.
Weeks-later review: a guided page that rereads the dream and sign logs after several weeks and marks each entry as held up, faded or probably coincidence, with a tally by kind.
Patterns page: themes, places and times of day that recur across both logs, and the symbols that earn a place in the symbol dictionary.
Going further: a second review a few months on, set beside the first to see what still stands.

chapters.title: Consent and Careful Words With a Partner
chapters.summary: Before any partner exercise, this chapter sets out the ethical framework for sharing impressions: consent, care with words, topics that stay off limits and no comparing progress. It comes before the partner exercises because how an impression is offered matters as much as what it is.
beats: Consent script: the words to ask a partner, what to explain (this is practice, not a reading), what they can decline, and how either person can stop at any time.
Off-limits list: no predictions or impressions about health, death, pregnancy or legal matters, never reading anyone without consent, and what to say if such an impression arrives anyway.
Careful-words rewrite drill: blunt or frightening phrasings rewritten as tentative, kind statements the reader owns, such as: I'm getting an image of a blue door; does that mean anything to you?
No comparing: a reflection page on measuring progress against friends, teachers or psychics on television, and on keeping the reader's own record as the only yardstick.
Going further: an agreement page for partners who practice together regularly, covering confidentiality and how feedback will be given.

chapters.title: Partner Exercises and Feedback Both Ways
chapters.summary: Simple exercises to run with a consenting partner, and a way to give and receive feedback that keeps both people honest and comfortable. It sits right after the ethics chapter so every exercise here runs inside that framework.
beats: Back-to-back exercise: partners sit back to back, one holds a simple image or feeling in mind, the other records what arrives, then they swap roles.
Hidden object exercise: the partner chooses an object out of sight, and the reader describes it sense by sense (shape, texture, use, feeling) before it is revealed.
Partner feedback form: what fitted, what did not, what was close, in the partner's own words, without coaching or rescuing the reader.
Receiving feedback: how to hear 'that doesn't fit' without arguing, explaining or stretching the impression, and how to keep partner scores separate from solo tests in the running record.
Going further: spend a session on the sending side and note how holding an image for someone changes the way the reader receives.

chapters.title: Meet a Guide, and Ask If It Feels Safe
chapters.summary: A guided meditation to meet a guide, questions for discernment (does it feel safe, kind and consistent) and pages to record each contact. The spiritual frame is taken seriously without a hierarchy of beings, and the chapter comes late because it needs a steady session frame and practice at telling impressions from noise.
beats: Preparing: a full opening from the session frame, a clear intention to meet only a guide that is safe and kind, and permission to stop at any moment.

Guided meditation in stages: a quiet path, a place of the reader's own choosing, an invitation, waiting without forcing, receiving whatever comes (a presence, an image, a word, or nothing yet) and a return through the closing.
Discernment questions after every contact: did it feel safe, kind and consistent, did it respect the reader's choices, did it flatter or frighten, and what to do if any answer is no.
Contact record pages: one layout for the first contact, another for later contacts, and a consistency summary across them (form, feeling, message, how the discernment questions came out).
What this practice leaves out: no ranking of guides, no other realms, no contact with the dead; a guide is one practice among others, not a requirement.
Going further: bring a clear question to the meeting and record the answer apart from the contact itself.

chapters.title: When Practice Stalls or Feels Like Too Much
chapters.summary: Doubt, plateaus, feeling too open and changes in sleep or mood can all come with practice; this chapter gives quick resets, clear signs for when to pause, and when to talk to a doctor or a therapist. It sits before the final plan so the reader builds their own routine knowing how to adjust it.
beats: Symptom finder: a page that matches what the reader notices (no impressions for weeks, constant doubt, feeling raw in crowds, restless sleep, low mood) to the reset or step that fits.
Quick resets menu: short grounding and closing practices for different moments (after a session, in a crowd, at night), each taking a few minutes.
Plateau page: a reflection on a stretch with no visible progress, rereading the running record and logs for small changes the reader may have missed, and choosing one change to try.
When to pause and when to get help: plain signs that mean stopping practice for a while, and signs that mean talking to a doctor or a therapist; this book never replaces either.
Going further: experienced practitioners write their own early-warning list from past periods of overload.

chapters.title: Your First Month, Planned Week by Week
chapters.summary: A four-week starter plan recombines the exercises of the book into short sessions, so the reader practices in a sensible order without deciding each time. It opens the closing section because a plan with a known shape is the step between doing exercises and keeping a practice.
beats: How the plan works: short sessions on chosen days, always inside the session frame, one main exercise and one log each time, with rest days built in.
Month at a glance: a calendar page to mark planned and completed sessions.

Week pages, each with its own focus and layout: week one settling and noticing; week two the senses; week three testing and questions; week four dreams, signs and symbols; each with a box to tick per session and a line for what stood out.
Swap rules: how to replace an exercise that isn't working with another from the same section, and when to repeat a week instead of moving on.
Going further: a harder version of each week for readers who already practice, such as longer silent sits or a partner test at the end of the week.

chapters.title: Design a Routine That Is Yours
chapters.summary: The reader designs a personal routine from the exercises that suited them, with a monthly review page to keep it honest and going further variations for those who already practice. It closes the book because the aim from the start was a practice the reader owns, not a program to follow.
beats: Routine builder: a page that pulls the reader's strongest sense, favorite exercises and best times from the profile chart, the running record and the logs, and assembles a weekly routine around a fixed session frame.
Personal practice agreement: how often, how long, which log stays and which rotates, when to rest, and what the reader will do after a break.
Monthly review page: what was practiced, what the records show, what has changed since the Experience Inventory and the first intentions, what to keep, drop or try next.
Going further for experienced practitioners: longer sessions, combining two senses in one exercise, blind tests with a partner, and a seasonal pass through the symbol dictionary.
Keeping the record going beyond the book, and coming back to the session frame after any pause without starting over.
